title: August and the Verdict
premise: When the coffin of August Verdict—founder of the town that bears his name—is opened for a centennial ceremony, it contains nothing but river stones and a century-old insurance policy made out to a woman who never officially existed. Ansel Brightwater, whose photographic memory makes her the county's most feared investigator, recognizes the handwriting on the policy as her own grandmother's, and realizes the town's founding legend is a fraud someone has spent a hundred years protecting. As Ansel digs into land deeds, drowned miners, and the town's founding families, she discovers the killer is the town archivist, who has been quietly erasing and rewriting the historical record for decades—and who now needs Ansel's perfect memory destroyed before she can testify to what the original documents said. In the flooded bell tower where August Verdict's real remains were hidden, Ansel traps the archivist into confessing on record, choosing at last to be seen rather than safe.
about_author: Felix Fairweather is a former small-town newspaper archivist who spent a decade cataloging municipal records and learning how much of history is a matter of careful filing. August and the Verdict is their fourth mystery and the first written under a name they chose themselves.

chapters.title: The Centennial Exhumation
chapters.summary: Ansel Brightwater attends the ceremonial opening of founder August Verdict's tomb, hired by the town council to verify the coffin's condition for an insurance claim. When the lid lifts to reveal river stones, her photographic memory captures every detail—the wrongness of the soil, the fresh chisel marks. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the thrill of an impossible case, undercut by dread.

chapters.title: A Policy for Nobody
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Ansel finds a life insurance policy dated 1898, payable to a woman named 'Lark Brightwater'—her grandmother's name, though her grandmother was born decades later. The archivist, Cordelia Moss, helpfully produces a file that contradicts Ansel's memory of the original. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the first crack in her trust in the record itself.

chapters.title: What the Stones Said
chapters.summary: Ansel interviews the gravedigger's grandson, who recalls his grandfather refusing, on his deathbed, to be buried in the Verdict cemetery. A flashback-tinged scene shows Ansel's childhood, when her grandmother taught her to memorize documents 'because paper lies.' POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: grief surfacing through professional detachment.

chapters.title: The Founder's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ansel reconstructs Verdict's mining-era ledger from memory and finds a page torn out—yet she can recite what it contained: a payment to 'L.' for silence. Councilman Harrow pressures her to close the case as vandalism. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the case turns personal; she refuses to let it go.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Ansel's colleague Deen notices someone accessed her office overnight, touching nothing but her case notes. Ansel realizes her reputation for never forgetting makes her a threat to whoever emptied the coffin. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: paranoia; invisibility was protection, now it's a target.

chapters.title: The Drowned Shaft
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's clues, Ansel explores a flooded mine shaft on the Verdict estate and finds a sealed strongbox wedged in the rock—too heavy to move alone. Someone watches her from the treeline; she catches only a smell of camphor. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: exhilaration shadowed by the certainty she's being managed.

chapters.title: Lark
chapters.summary: Ansel visits her estranged aunt and learns the family secret: Lark Brightwater was a real woman, a miner's widow paid off after a collapse that killed eleven men—a collapse the town blamed on her husband. POV: aunt's recollection framed by Ansel. Emotional beat: her belonging to this town was built on a buried crime.

chapters.title: Cordelia's Kindness
chapters.summary: The archivist Cordelia brings Ansel tea and a newly 'discovered' document exonerating August Verdict entirely. Ansel's memory flags the paper stock as modern. She says nothing, and Cordelia's smile lingers a beat too long. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing her ally is her adversary.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Ansel's insurance firm, spooked by council pressure, gives her two weeks before the claim closes and evidence gets sealed. She begins copying everything she knows into a notebook she can leave behind—in case her memory stops being believed. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: racing the clock; the loneliness of being the only witness.

chapters.title: The Bell Tower Flood
chapters.summary: Ansel maps the old church records and realizes the bell tower's flooded crypt connects to the mine shafts—the strongbox's contents could be reached from below. She also finds the crypt was sealed in 1974, the year her grandmother left town. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the pieces aligning into a shape she almost doesn't want to see.

chapters.title: Harrow's Bargain
chapters.summary: Councilman Harrow offers Ansel a lifetime contract and a quiet apology fund if she declares the case unsolvable. She records the offer, and he laughs: 'Who believes a memory without a page?' POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: rage crystallizing into strategy.

chapters.title: Camphor and Dust
chapters.summary: Ansel stakes out the archive at night and catches Cordelia substituting a forged ledger page. Confronted, Cordelia doesn't deny it—she warns Ansel that the founding families have killed to keep this buried, and that Cordelia is only the latest keeper of the lie. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; the villain claims to be a curator.

chapters.title: Eleven Names
chapters.summary: From memory, Ansel recites the eleven miners who died in the collapse and cross-references their descendants: half the town council, the gravedigger's family, her own. The empty coffin wasn't theft—it was a message, placed by someone returning the stones from the shaft. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the town itself becomes the suspect.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Confession
chapters.summary: Cordelia reveals the archivist's role: every generation, one keeper rewrites the record to protect the families, and the keeper is always chosen for a perfect memory—like Ansel was meant to be. Lark Brightwater refused the role in 1974 and was driven out. POV: Cordelia's account, Ansel's frame. Emotional beat: Ansel sees her own inheritance of complicity.

chapters.title: Deen Disappears
chapters.summary: Deen, who took the strongbox coordinates from Ansel's notes, goes missing. Ansel's notebook is stolen from her car—the thief wanted her to feel the theft, to doubt her backup. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: fear turning to fury; they've made it personal twice.

chapters.title: Into the Crypt
chapters.summary: Ansel dives the flooded crypt alone, finds the strongbox open and empty except for Lark Brightwater's original testimony—a sworn statement about the collapse, signed by eleven widows. Taped to it, a note in Cordelia's hand: 'Bring the memory. Come alone.' POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the trap is sprung, and she walks into it willingly.

chapters.title: The Trial Below
chapters.summary: In the bell tower, Cordelia and Harrow await Ansel with the stolen notebook and a demand: recant her findings publicly, or be discredited as unstable—her photographic memory recast as confabulation. Ansel stalls, asking questions, keeping them talking. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: terror harnessed into performance.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Ansel reveals she's been recording since she entered the crypt—Deen, freed and hiding in the rafters, holds the second recorder. Cordelia breaks: the keeper before her was her mother, and the empty coffin was her own act of conscience, forcing the lie into the light. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the confession, and unexpected grief for her enemy.

chapters.title: Harrow's Fall
chapters.summary: Harrow tries to destroy the record and is arrested as the recordings and the widows' testimony go to the state attorney. The founding families' descendants, confronted with the eleven names, begin to fracture—some confess, some flee, one offers Ansel the archive itself. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: vindication without satisfaction.

chapters.title: Reinterment
chapters.summary: The real remains of the collapse victims are recovered from the shaft and buried with their names read aloud. Ansel recites the eleven names from memory at the service, and the town listens. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: mourning as public act; belonging, at last, on honest terms.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Chair
chapters.summary: Ansel is offered Cordelia's post as town archivist and declines—but negotiates instead an independent records commission with herself as outside auditor, so no keeper ever again works alone. Cordelia, awaiting trial, sends her the original 1898 policy as a gift. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: power accepted with safeguards; memory put in service.

chapters.title: August, Closing
chapters.summary: Ansel closes the insurance file with a verdict no one expected: the coffin was empty because the town never actually buried what happened. On the train out, she memorizes one last document—her own resignation—and lets herself forget the exact wording, choosing to live forward. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: release; a perfect memory learning the grace of letting go.
